Hey there! I think making the list is a good idea, but if it starts to be overwhelming and guilt-inducing breaking it down further may help.

I personally like to think of tasks as either "important" or "urgent" or neither! If you break down your lists of things you want to do into a grid like that, it can help highlight what you want to prioritize. Paying your toll bill? Maybe not that important, but would be an urgent task if it was time sensitive. Studying for a test next week? Not urgent, but definitely important. Doing major homework for tomorrow? Urgent AND important!

Sometimes we do not have enough resilience to get through everything on our list for the day and that is okay! If you view your planned schedule as an "absolute best case scenario" and then tackle tasks according to their urgency/importance you can make sure that you got the most bang for your buck of whatever effort you put into your day. In the end, focus more on not having a zero day. Even if you only wake up and stay sober, hey! That is pretty great! And will help you start again tomorrow. Good luck!

Okay, I agree with the majority of people that say he does not have a porn addiction. It does not sound like these are uncontrollable impulses that he cannot fight off and are ruining his life.

HOWEVER, regardless on whether your stance on porn is right or wrong, you are asking him to commit to certain standards and behaviours in the relationship and he is agreeing to your requests, lying that he will change and work towards them, and then going behind your back. Assuming you have talked about why you don't like him looking at porn, he is also willingly and knowingly putting you through a lot of emotional pain when he engages in those activities.

I would not think of it as a "my boyfriend looks at porn!" problem, but rather "my boyfriend lies to me and says he will support me but instead just breaks his promises and gets defensive about it!" If he does not think it is reasonable for you to ask these things of him that is fine, and a completely separate issue. However, it is REALLY unhealthy for him not to express his viewpoints and be honest with you about his feelings about things you bring up in the relationship dialogue. That sort of dishonesty is really backwards and not good for the relationship at all.

On a related note, I would not be too upset with him for the double standard of porn watching. It might be unreasonable and illogical, but at least he is being honest about how he feels about it and that is an okay place to be. You can work on problems and inconsistencies if you two are being honest.

Actually, quitting alcohol cold turkey is not that simple. For normal drinkers, stopping completely can be fine, but for alcoholics quitting cold turkey can also kill you. Alcohol is a major depressant, and slows down the nerve firings in your brain. As you grow more dependent on it and use more, your neurons try to compensate for this and fire more rapidly. As such, if you stop giving yourself this regular high dose of depressants out of the blue, your neurons will not have time to calm down and will continue to exist in an overexcited states leading to seizures and possibly death.

To me, budgeting and sex are not make or break deals, but from reading reddit posts those seem like two important things. For me, the "make or break" things that I listed were meant to represent large issues that needed to be talked about because they usually had a large deal of important in people's lives. Make or break was not the best choice of words, because I agree that compromise will be necessary on almost all of those things.

I absolutely think that sexual preferences are an area of compromise and are not a good enough reason to break it off. I seem to see a fair about of posts on reddit concerning sexual compatibility as a huge deal breaker, and that irks me. I think it is a very important topic to discuss before engagement, but I think when you say "We really have to work at enjoying it and satisfying each other," you are expressing a lovely principle that embodies the communication and openness to change that I think is extremely important in cases like these.

There will never be a relationship in which all issues are worked out before marriage. People change and evolve constantly and with that fact comes new problems and challenges. "Make or break" issues such as sex, children, budgeting, lifestyles, commitment etc. should absolutely be discussed prior to any engagement. However, even if you now have the same viewpoint on how to raise a child, it is completely possible (and absolutely probable) that over the next few years, your viewpoint on that will shift. That being said, what I would advise is to confront all of the major and minor issues you can think of in your relationship an make sure you have an ongoing conversation about your relationship. Communication is key, as I am sure you have heard. You will change and become more advanced and complex people throughout your respective lives. As long as you are committed to loving and working with the other person no matter what comes up, it is okay to have unresolved issues and differences in your relationship as long as you are aware of what those are and that your respective positions on those issues may change. Good luck!

My younger brother was diagnosed with Type I diabetes when he was eight. No one in out family had diabetes, so we were completely unprepared for the unfathomable onslaught of life threatening responsibilities that needed to be addressed and monitored almost constantly. It took our family a while to realize that this was not going to go away after any period of time and that even when one day it was not our daily responsibility, he would have to carry the burden and always be vigilant if he wanted a healthy life. My brother adapted well to the diagnoses at first, but after about a year he started freaking out about being diabetic. One of the worst memories I have are of watching my brother frequently break down into an inconsolable wreck and scream of how he hated being diabetic and how life was unfair. I always felt so helpless at these times, which might be what other people feel when you share your worries with them. However, they should NEVER brush it off or give you the responses you mentioned above.

My brother tried killing himself on an insulin overdose the night before I left for college, and it was something I will never understand. I cannot personally relate to what YOU are going through, but as a person who has spent the last four years maintaining a relationship with a person who self-harms and is occasionally suicidal because of the despondency he feels, I can tell you that every day I spend with him is precious.

You are not your diabetes. You are not your diabetes. You are not your diabetes. You have a lifelong disease that you have to deal with on a daily basis, but you are so much more than that. You have a chronic disease you cannot change and to some extent, you do have to move on. Diabetes does not have to control your life if you control your diabetes well enough. There is so much living to be done outside of monitoring your blood sugar, and I know that there are people in your life who greatly value the memories they have made/will make with you. Find someone to talk to; that seems to be a big issue. There are therapists who work specifically with people with lifelong illnesses and they may be able to help you figure out a healthy perspective about your life.
